transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I’m here because I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t. Like heart follow-up appointments, or I forget to call the clinic back. Even with repair jobs, I’ll show up and realize I didn’t bring the right tools. It’s been happening enough that I figured I should talk to somebody about it.
Have these forgetfulness problems gotten worse compared with how you used to be?

Yeah, I’d say it’s been happening more than it used to, or at least it’s causing more trouble now. I mean, forgetting heart follow-up appointments, not calling the clinic back, or showing up to a repair job without the right tools—that’s the kind of thing that’s been getting hard to ignore.
When you were a child, did you often have trouble paying attention or staying organized?

Yeah, I did. In grade school I was always the kid who couldn’t sit still. I’d blurt out answers before I was supposed to, and I got notes sent home for talking too much. Staying in my seat was a problem.
As an adult, have you consistently had trouble staying organized?
I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean, I know I forget things and lose track sometimes, but as far as being consistently disorganized as an adult… I haven’t really thought of it that way.
Before age 12, did you often lose things or forget what you were supposed to do?

I don’t remember so much about losing things or forgetting tasks specifically. What I do remember is, in grade school I was always getting in trouble for not staying in my seat, blurting out answers, and talking too much. Notes got sent home for that pretty often.
Have these memory problems been steadily getting worse over time?

I’m not sure I’d say steadily worse, but it’s gotten noticeable enough that it’s why I’m here. I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t — like heart follow-up appointments, calling the clinic back, or even showing up to a repair job without the right tools. It’s frustrating.
As a teenager, were you still having trouble sitting still or blurting things out?

I’m not sure about my teenage years specifically, but I know even back in grade school I was that kid who couldn’t stay in his seat. I’d blurt out answers, talk too much, and notes got sent home about it.
Do you need help from other people to manage your daily activities?

Yeah, more than I’d like to admit. The senior-center repair group can’t really count on me the way they used to, and my doctor’s office has had to call and chase me down about missed heart follow-ups. So I’m not helpless, but I do seem to need people reminding me or following up.
Have you gotten lost in places that used to be familiar to you?
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed getting lost in places I know. If I’m somewhere unfamiliar, sure, I might have to think about it, but familiar places haven’t been a problem that I can tell.
Did these memory problems first start after you were older?

No, I don’t think it was just something that started when I got older. Like I said, even back in grade school I was the kid who couldn’t stay in his seat, blurted things out, and got notes sent home for talking too much.
Have you been feeling depressed most days?
I’m not really sure I’d say depressed most days. I get frustrated with myself, but I haven’t been thinking of it as feeling depressed day after day.
Compared with how you used to be at your best as an adult, do you feel your memory and thinking have clearly declined?

I’m not sure I’d call it a clear decline. I mean, I forget things here and there, but compared to when I was younger or at my best as an adult, I haven’t really noticed a big change in my memory or thinking.
Do you worry a lot about many different things?
I don’t think so. I mean, I worry about normal stuff, but I wouldn’t say it’s a lot of different things all the time.
Has anyone close to you told you that your memory or thinking has gotten worse than it used to be?

No, not really. I mean, nobody close to me has sat me down and said my memory or thinking is getting worse. Maybe they remind me about things sometimes, but I don’t think anyone’s made a big point of it.
Has there been a clear change in your memory or thinking compared with how you usually were as an adult?
Not that I can tell. I mean, I have the usual forgetful moments, but I don’t feel like there’s been some clear change from how I’ve generally been as an adult.
Has a family member or close friend noticed that your memory or thinking is getting worse over time?
No, I don’t think so. My family or close friends haven’t told me they think my memory or thinking is getting worse over time.
Did your current memory problems begin after you developed your heart condition?

Yes, it was after that heart scare. The memory trouble’s been a real problem for about a year and a couple months now, since I had to cut back on the walking and projects that used to keep me more settled.
Did your forgetfulness start soon after your heart scare?

Yes, pretty soon after that, as best I can tell. It’s been causing real trouble for about a year and two months now, since that heart scare made me cut back on the walking and projects that used to keep me settled.
Did you have a stroke around the time of your heart scare?
I’m not sure. I don’t remember anyone telling me I had a stroke then, but I’d have to check to be certain.
Around the time of your heart scare, were you suddenly confused for a while?
I don’t really know. I don’t remember being suddenly confused like that, but I may not be the best judge of it. No one told me I was, as far as I can recall.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a new period of clinically significant forgetfulness beginning soon after a heart-related medical event and lasting about 14 months, with need for reminders and reduced reliability in daily responsibilities. This pattern supports mild cognitive disorder due to a known physiological condition more than ADHD or unspecified dementia. ADHD is considered because of clear childhood hyperactivity/impulsivity, but there is insufficient evidence of persistent adult syndrome with the required inattention pattern. Unspecified dementia is less likely because there is no clear progressive decline, no disorientation in familiar places, and impairment appears mild rather than major.
